title: The shelf it was aimed at
lede: OK was built to take share from the sodas teenagers already drank, above all Mountain Dew. Its closest relatives were Coca-Cola’s own experiments.

blocks.title: Six drinks from Coca-Cola’s and Pepsi’s 1993–1994 line-ups
blocks.subtitle: What each was, and what became of it.

items.name: OK Soda
items.text: Sold in test markets from May 1994; phased out from September 1995.[^9]

items.name: Mountain Dew
items.text: Pepsi’s citrus soda and the most popular drink aimed at teenagers in 1994, by share of the US market.[^6]

items.name: Mello Yello
items.text: Coca-Cola’s existing answer to Mountain Dew.[^6]

items.name: Sprite
items.text: Given a new campaign that year, “Obey Your Thirst,” which Time called highly successful.[^6]

items.name: Fruitopia
items.text: Coca-Cola’s rival to Snapple, launched the same year.[^13] Phased out in the United States in 2003, by a later account.[^20]

items.name: Tab Clear
items.text: In Coca-Cola’s product list for 1993 and absent from the list for 1994.[^2][^1]

blocks.source: Time, May 30, 1994[^6]; The New York Times[^9]; The Believer[^13]; Coca-Cola Forms 10-K for 1993 and 1994[^2][^1]; The Takeout[^20]. The OK sparkline is the count of reported test cities from the numbers section.

left.name: OK Soda
rows: Eight or nine US test cities[^6][^8]

right.name: Fruitopia
rows: Not in the sources we read
In the product list after OK left it; phased out in the US in 2003[^3][^20]

blocks.title: The same year, the opposite mood
blocks.body: The Believer sets the two launches side by side. Fruitopia “drew on the sunnier side of indie culture,” with kaleidoscopic fruit and flavors called Strawberry Passion Awareness, and “remained popular throughout the ’90s.” OK’s graphics came in “stoic grays and reds.”[^13] One advertising executive told Time in 1994 that teenagers had enough to be “bummed out about” and did not want to be reminded of it.[^6]
